name: Ab wheel

lead: An ab wheel, or ab roller, is a small wheel on an axle with a handle on each side. The user kneels, rolls the wheel forward until the body is extended, then pulls back. People use it to build thicker, stronger abs for a more defined midsection.

As the wheel rolls out, the lever arm lengthens and the abdominal muscles resist the spine arching, loading the rectus abdominis, obliques and deep core, with lats and shoulders also working. Electromyography studies of similar exercises show high abdominal activity. How visible the abs are depends heavily on body fat level, so the wheel is used to build the muscle while diet handles the rest.

paras: Users add rollouts at the end of workouts, starting with a partial range or a wall stop and building up distance. It is combined with a diet aimed at getting lean so the abs show.

Lower-back sag, shoulder strain and wrist discomfort are the common problems, and the exercise is hard for many beginners. People with back or shoulder issues are generally advised to take care. Spot training has not been shown to reliably reduce fat from one area.

angle.text: Users roll an ab wheel to train the core hard and build thicker abdominal muscles, which show as defined abs once body fat is low. Core activation during such exercises has been measured; forum posters commonly note that diet drives how visible the abs are.

lead: The ab wheel, also called an ab roller, is a small home exercise device made of a wheel on an axle with a handle on each side. The user kneels or stands, grips the handles and rolls the wheel forward and back, which loads the abdominal muscles to build a stronger, more developed midsection.[1]

People use it for the looks goal of a defined, visible core. Rolling out lengthens the lever arm so the abdominal muscles must resist the trunk extending, working the rectus abdominis, obliques and deep abdominal muscles, with the shoulders and lats stabilising.[1] Larger, better-developed abdominal muscles show more clearly when body fat is low.
A 2006 electromyography study in Physical Therapy compared traditional and non-traditional abdominal exercises for training and rehabilitation.[2]

paras: Basic components are a wheel, an axle and handles. Wheels are generally rubber or plastic with a textured tread, axles are steel, and handles carry foam or rubber grips [1]. Some models include sealed bearings for smoother rolling [1].

Dual-wheel designs have two wheels side by side on a shared axle and are described as more stable laterally, which makes them more forgiving for beginners [1]. Single-wheel designs require more balance and are described as harder [1]. Some products add a return spring or a knee pad.

According to one source, wheel-based exercise devices were patented in the 1930s, mainly for lower-back exercises, and a commercial product called the Reduce-A-Wheel appeared in the United States in the 1960s [1]. The Abdominizer, a non-wheel device invented in 1984 by a Canadian chiropractor, is cited as another earlier abdominal product [1].

The same source dates the modern Ab Roller to 1994 and credits its popularity to mid-1990s infomercials, with the manufacturer claiming more than 10 million units sold and over $1 billion in revenue [1]. These dates and figures come from a machine-written encyclopedia and have not been independently verified.

As the wheel moves away from the body, the lever arm grows and the abdominal muscles must resist the trunk extending. This loads the rectus abdominis, obliques and deep abdominal muscles, with the shoulders and lats stabilising and controlling the return [1]. Range of motion, starting position (kneeling versus standing) and wheel design change the difficulty.

A 2006 study in Physical Therapy used electromyography to compare traditional and non-traditional abdominal exercises, with implications for training and rehabilitation [2]. Wider fitness-writing sources describe ab wheel rollouts as producing higher abdominal muscle activation than some traditional exercises [1], but no peer-reviewed study of the plain kneeling rollout was identified in the material reviewed.

Wikipedia's spot reduction article reports a randomized study of 24 sedentary adults aged 18 to 40 in which a group added seven abdominal exercises for six weeks. Their abdominal subcutaneous fat did not decrease while core muscular endurance improved, and the article states that fat is lost from the whole body through diet and exercise rather than from targeted areas.[3] Changes in how visible the abdominal muscles are therefore depend mainly on overall body fat.

Commonly reported problems include lower-back sagging into extension, shoulder strain and wrist discomfort. The exercise is demanding, and beginners often use a shortened range, a wall stop or a dual-wheel model. People with back or shoulder conditions are generally advised by trainers to be cautious. One source asserts that proper use reduces back-injury risk by training spinal stabilisation [1]; that claim has not been tested in trials identified here.
No studies found on the ab wheel as a product for appearance outcomes. A related laboratory study compared electromyographic activity across traditional and non-traditional abdominal exercises [2].

The ab wheel is discussed as an inexpensive way to train the abdominal wall at home. The common framing in fitness communities is that the muscle can be developed with training while visible definition depends on diet and body fat.
